```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _lib.orplot import COLORS, mark_point
from _lib.toy_network import ARCS, NODES, POS, min_cost_flow, draw_network

AMOUNT = 12
sol = min_cost_flow(AMOUNT)
flow = {(u, v): sol["x"][j] for j, (u, v, *_) in enumerate(ARCS)}
pi = sol["potential"]
```

## The idea

Combine the two previous problems. Each arc now has a **cost per unit** and a
**capacity**, and we must ship a given amount from $s$ to $t$ (or, more generally,
from supply nodes to demand nodes) at the least total cost.

In the toy network, the cheapest way to ship $12$ units costs $112$. The first units
go along the shortest path ($8$ per unit), but its arcs fill up, and later units must
take more expensive routes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mcf
#| fig-cap: "A minimum-cost flow of 12 units in the toy network; each arc shows flow / capacity (costs are those on the Shortest Paths page). The blue number next to each node is its potential $\\pi_v$, the dual price of one more unit at that node. Arcs carry flow only when they are \"worth it\" at these prices: see the optimality conditions below."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.7))
draw_network(ax, label={(u, v): f"{flow[(u, v)]:g}/{k}" for u, v, w, k in ARCS},
             dim=[e for e in flow if flow[e] < 1e-9])
for v in NODES:
    x, y = POS[v]
    ax.text(x, y + (0.27 if y > 0.5 else -0.36), f"{round(pi[v], 6) + 0:g}", ha="center", fontsize=10,
            color=COLORS["p1"], fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

## The math

### The model

Let each node $v$ have a **supply** $b_v$ (positive at sources, negative at sinks, zero
at transshipment nodes, summing to zero). With costs $c_{ij}$ and capacities $u_{ij}$:
$$
\min \sum_{(i,j)} c_{ij} x_{ij}
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\sum_{j} x_{ij} - \sum_{j} x_{ji} = b_i \ \ \text{for every node } i,
\qquad 0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}.
$$
Many classical problems are special cases:

| Problem | How it fits |
|---|---|
| [Shortest path](shortest-paths.qmd) | supply 1 at $s$, demand 1 at $t$, no capacities |
| [Maximum flow](max-flow-min-cut.qmd) | cost 0 on all arcs, plus a return arc $t \to s$ with cost $-1$ |
| Transportation [@hitchcock1941] | supply nodes connected directly to demand nodes |
| Assignment | transportation with all supplies and demands equal to 1 |

### Optimality: no negative cycles

Given a feasible flow, look at its residual network: forward arcs keep cost $c_{ij}$,
backward arcs (cancelling flow) get cost $-c_{ij}$. A cycle of negative total cost in
the residual network is a way to reroute flow and save money while still meeting all
supplies and demands.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (negative-cycle optimality)
A feasible flow is a minimum-cost flow if and only if its residual network contains no
cycle of negative cost.
:::

This gives the **cycle-canceling** algorithm of @klein1967: start from any feasible flow
(for example, from a max-flow computation), and as long as a negative cycle exists, push
flow around it.

### Optimality: potentials and reduced costs

The dual LP assigns a **potential** $\pi_v$ to each node, as for shortest paths. The
**reduced cost** of an arc is $\bar c_{ij} = c_{ij} + \pi_i - \pi_j$, its cost after
paying $\pi_i$ to take a unit at $i$ and receiving $\pi_j$ for delivering it at $j$.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (reduced-cost optimality)
A feasible flow $x$ is optimal if and only if there are potentials $\pi$ such that for
every arc:
$$
\bar c_{ij} > 0 \Rightarrow x_{ij} = 0, \qquad
\bar c_{ij} < 0 \Rightarrow x_{ij} = u_{ij}, \qquad
0 < x_{ij} < u_{ij} \Rightarrow \bar c_{ij} = 0 .
$$
:::

This is [complementary slackness](../../linear-programming/duality/lp-duality.qmd) for
the min-cost flow LP. In the figure: $s \to b$ has $\bar c = 4 + 0 - 3 = 1 > 0$ and
carries nothing; $a \to c$ has $\bar c = 7 + 2 - 10 = -1 < 0$ and is full; $d \to t$ has
$\bar c = 5 + 6 - 11 = 0$ and is partly used.

### The cost of shipping more is convex

Let $C(k)$ be the minimum cost of shipping $k$ units. It is convex and piecewise linear,
like every LP [value function](../../linear-programming/duality/sensitivity-analysis.qmd).
Its slope at $k$ is the cost of the cheapest augmenting path in the residual network of
the optimal $k$-unit flow: the marginal cost of one more unit.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mcf-cost
#| fig-cap: "Minimum cost $C(k)$ of shipping $k$ units from $s$ to $t$ in the toy network, up to the maximum flow 18. The marginal cost per unit rises from 8 (the shortest path) to 12 as cheap arcs fill up. The red dot is the 12-unit flow shown above."
K = np.arange(0, 19)
Ck = np.array([min_cost_flow(k)["cost"] for k in K])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.5))
ax.plot(K, Ck, color=COLORS["p1"], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
mark_point(ax, (AMOUNT, sol["cost"]), COLORS["weak"])
slopes = np.diff(Ck)
for k0, k1 in [(0, 4), (5, 11), (12, 18)]:
    km = (k0 + k1) / 2
    ax.text(km - 0.3, np.interp(km, K, Ck) + 14, f"{slopes[k0]:g} per unit", fontsize=9,
            ha="center", color=COLORS["p1"])
ax.set_xlabel("units shipped, $k$"); ax.set_ylabel("minimum cost $C(k)$")
ax.set_xlim(0, 18.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 205); ax.set_xticks(range(0, 19, 3))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (integrality)
If all supplies and capacities are integers and the problem is feasible, there is an
optimal flow with integer values on every arc.
:::

So "ship whole trucks" or "assign whole people" never needs integer programming when
the problem is a min-cost flow. The reason is
[total unimodularity](../integrality-and-matching/total-unimodularity.qmd).

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: negative cycles
If the residual network has a negative cycle, pushing a small amount around it keeps
every supply and demand satisfied and every capacity respected, and lowers the cost, so
the flow was not optimal.

Conversely, if $x$ is feasible but not optimal, let $x^\star$ be optimal. The difference
$x^\star - x$ satisfies "zero net supply" at every node, so it decomposes into flow around
cycles, each of which is a cycle in the residual network of $x$. Their costs add up to
$c^\top x^\star - c^\top x < 0$, so at least one of them is negative.
:::

## In practice

- **Very large instances are routine.** The simplex method [@dantzig1951] specialized to
  networks, where a basis is a spanning tree, and dedicated combinatorial algorithms solve
  min-cost flow problems with millions of arcs.
- **Logistics and distribution** models (plants, warehouses, customers, with shipping
  costs and capacities) are min-cost flow problems, as long as there are no fixed costs
  or other logic. Fixed costs make them integer programs.
- **As a building block.** Min-cost flow is the subproblem in many decompositions and
  the LP relaxation of many network design problems.
